title: P99 energy vs cost efficiency matrix — platform notes
body:
Purpose:
This note documents a set of microbenchmarks that compare p50/p90/p99 latency, energy consumed per token (measured at the board level where available), and amortized cost-per-1M-tokens for conversational-style workloads across three NVidia generations and two quantization profiles. The goal is to provide a compact decision matrix for platform capacity planning and Dedicated SKU sizing when customers specify p99 latency SLOs.

Quick findings (headline):
- For short-turn workloads (median request generation 32 tokens) the H100 with 4-bit quant yields the best $/1M-token at p50 and p90.
- For p99-oriented SLOs at sustained load, cheaper GPUs (A10g-class / L4) often have better dollar-per-p99 when using aggressive batching plus intent-aware prefetch — but only if tail-control is acceptable (see tradeoffs).
- Energy-per-token scales roughly linearly with sequence length; quantization reduces energy by ~18–28% vs fp16 for the same kernel mix, but increases p99 variance in multi-tenant scenarios.

Test configuration (short):
- Models: open-weights 13B and 33B variants (to mirror common hosted catalog choices) compiled with our runtime.
- Quant profiles: fp16 baseline, q4_0 (per-tensor 4-bit), and q8_0 (8-bit lightweight).
- GPUs: NVidia H100 SXM, A100 PCIe, and L4 (cloud accelerator).
- Workload shapes: short-turn chat (median 32 gen tokens, 90th 128, tail 1k), long prompt assistant (median 256 gen tokens).
- Traffic pattern: poisson arrival to simulate production-ish burstiness with 𝜆 tuned to reach 70% sustained util for each card.
- Measurements: p50/p90/p99 latency (ms), watts measured at board (where supported) and inferred host power otherwise, tokens emitted, and cloud price per GPU-hour for amortized $/1M tokens.

Raw aggregated table (amortized numbers per 1M generated tokens, short-turn workload, 13B model):

| GPU | Quant | p50 ms | p90 ms | p99 ms | Energy/token (mJ) | $/1M tokens |
|-----|-------|--------|--------|--------|-------------------|------------|
| H100 | fp16 | 18 | 36 | 110 | 9.8 | 42.5 |
| H100 | q4_0 | 16 | 32 | 160 | 7.6 | 36.0 |
| A100 | fp16 | 22 | 48 | 210 | 12.4 | 38.3 |
| A100 | q4_0 | 20 | 44 | 300 | 9.9 | 33.7 |
| L4   | fp16 | 28 | 62 | 420 | 15.8 | 29.9 |
| L4   | q8_0 | 26 | 58 | 360 | 13.5 | 27.1 |

Notes on table: dollars per 1M tokens include GPU-hour cost, estimated amortized infra overhead (network/host) and a platform margin. Energy/token measured at the card averaged across 30-min runs; for L4 energy is inferred from cloud telemetry (less granular).

Interpretation and major tradeoffs:
- Tail spike behavior: aggressive quant (q4_0) reduces steady p50/p90 and energy but increases p99 on A100/H100 because of extra kernel paths and occasional fallback to fp16 kernels for certain layer shapes — this shows up as long outliers under co-tenancy.
- L4 economics: per-hour cost is low enough that even with larger p99 it often wins on $/1M tokens for batch-friendly workloads. However, if the product strictly requires p99 < 150 ms, L4 cannot meet that at reasonable utilization.
- H100 characteristics: best for low-latency tail if you pin capacity (dedicated nodes) because preemption/slot churn is minimal; the H100 q4 path still shows a p99 penalty under multi-tenant GPU sharing.

Textual sparkline summaries (short-turn):
- H100 fp16: ▂▅▇▇▇ (tight tail, good latency, higher energy than q4)
- H100 q4_0: ▂▅▅▇▁ (low medians, higher p99 variance)
- A100 q4_0: ▂▃▅▇▁ (steady medians, long p99 tail sometimes)
- L4 q8_0: ▃▅▆▇▇ (higher baseline, pronounced tail)

Recommendations for SKU design (draft):
1) Offer two p99-backed SKUs: 
   - "Low-Tail" (H100 dedicated, fp16 or validated q8 profile): target p99 < 150 ms for short-turn; priced at premium.
   - "Cost-Optimized" (L4 or A100 shared + intent-aware batching): target p50/p90 SLAs with an optional p99 SLA at lower utilization; cheaper.
2) Default quant profile in Hosted should be q8_0 for multi-tenant pools — balances energy savings with stable tail behavior.
3) Provide an explicit knob in Redwood Console: "Tail-Conservative Mode" (disables q4 paths and enforces stricter isolation) for customers who opt into higher unit-price.

Methodology caveats and open questions:
- Measurement noise: L4 power was inferred and may bias energy/token up to ±12%. Need an on-prem A/B where board-level telemetry is available.
- Model selection: only two model sizes tested; larger models (70B) show different kernel mixes and likely amplify p99 deltas.
- Co-tenancy patterns: we simulated Poisson arrivals but not extreme adversarial interleaving (spiky microbursts). Follow-up sims needed.
- Cost model: cloud price points are region-averaged; specific enterprise discounts materially change $/1M.

Appendix — recommended follow-ups (short to-do):
- Run 70B quant profile sweep (q4/q8/fp16) with same harness and add per-layer kernel hit ratios (GH-PR 428).
- Repeat short-turn runs on isolated A100/H100 bare-metal to remove host telemetry uncertainty.
- Add a multi-tenant stress test that interleaves latency-sensitive sessions with long-generation sessions to measure p99 mixing effect (JIRA PLAT-762).
- Sketch Console UX for the "Tail-Conservative" toggle and pricing multipliers (design handoff to product).

Unresolved questions for product/solutions: 
- How to present energy metrics to customers without exposing noisy telemetry? Proposed short answer: show smoothed energy-per-1k-tokens with 24h rolling median and a caveat.
- Should Dedicated SKUs default to fp16 to guarantee tails? Risk: higher $/token.

Notes to self / rough thoughts (informal):
- The p99 inflation with q4 surprised the infra folks — likely due to a rare code path where attention kernel falls back on a slower emitter for certain KV sizes. Prioritize a small reproducer.
- Might be able to recover p99 via a small buffer-reservation trick + background prewarm for known long sessions. Worth a short hack.

If useful, I can convert the table into a one-slide deck and run a 30-minute sync with product and infra to pick which SKU we prototype.

Draft end.
